result.overall: The Court dismissed Ms. Ambroise's application for judicial review, finding the RAD's IFA analysis reasonable and no breach of procedural fairness, as she had a fair opportunity to respond.

themes.name: Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) Analysis
themes.summary: The Court focused on whether the RAD reasonably found Cap-Haïtien to be a viable IFA for Ms. Ambroise, considering both risk and reasonableness prongs.

themes.name: Risk of Persecution and State Protection
themes.summary: The Court examined whether Ms. Ambroise faced a serious possibility of persecution or danger in Cap-Haïtien, and whether the RAD needed to analyze state protection.

themes.name: Procedural Fairness
themes.summary: The Court considered whether the RPD breached procedural fairness by not raising the IFA issue at the outset of the hearing.

themes.name: Employment and Reasonableness of IFA
themes.summary: The Court addressed whether lack of employment in Ms. Ambroise's profession made the IFA unreasonable.

themes.name: Standard of Review
themes.summary: The Court clarified the applicable standards of review for IFA reasonableness and procedural fairness issues.

arguments.claim: The RAD failed to recognize that state protection for women is lacking throughout Haiti and should have analyzed state protection before concluding there was an IFA.
arguments.quote: the RAD should have analyzed the effectiveness of state protection before it concluded that there was an IFA. I reject this argument.

arguments.claim: The IFA would be unreasonable because Ms. Ambroise would face a serious risk of sexual violence and could not obtain employment as a nurse.
arguments.quote: the inability to find employment as a nurse would not put Ms. Ambroise’s life or safety at risk

arguments.claim: The RAD’s decision breached procedural fairness because the RPD failed to state at the outset of the hearing that an IFA would be raised.
arguments.quote: procedural fairness does not require that an IFA be raised at the outset of the hearing

arguments.claim: Ms. Ambroise failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution in Cap-Haïtien or that it would be unreasonable for her to relocate there.
arguments.quote: the RAD reasonably concluded that Ms. Ambroise failed to discharge that burden.

holdings.statement: Reasonableness applies to the RAD’s IFA determination; correctness (or fairness) applies to procedural fairness issues.
holdings.quote: the standard that applies to the second issue is the standard that applies to issues of procedural fairness

holdings.statement: To rebut an IFA, a claimant must show (1) a serious possibility of persecution or risk in the IFA, and (2) that relocation would be unreasonable.
holdings.quote: a claimant must satisfy the RAD, on a balance of probabilities, that (1) the claimant will be subject to persecution... and (2)... conditions in the IFA are such that it would be unreasonable

holdings.statement: The RAD’s analysis and conclusion that Cap-Haïtien is a viable IFA for Ms. Ambroise was reasonable.
holdings.quote: The RAD reasonably concluded that Ms. Ambroise failed to discharge that burden.

holdings.statement: There was no breach of procedural fairness in how the IFA issue was raised at the RPD hearing.
holdings.quote: I cannot conclude that there was a breach of procedural fairness.

holdings.statement: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
holdings.quote: the application for judicial review is dismissed.

rebuttals.point: The RAD should have analyzed state protection before concluding there was an IFA.
rebuttals.court_answer: The RAD was not required to analyze state protection because it found no serious possibility of persecution in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.quote: the RAD was not required to analyze state protection.

rebuttals.point: The RAD’s conclusion is unreasonable given evidence of sexual violence and criminal impunity in Haiti.
rebuttals.court_answer: The RAD considered the evidence and reasonably found no serious possibility of persecution for Ms. Ambroise in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.quote: it was not unreasonable for the RAD to determine that... there was not a “serious possibility” that Ms. Ambroise would face persecution

rebuttals.point: The RAD’s conclusion is unreasonable because of lack of employment opportunities in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.court_answer: The inability to find employment as a nurse does not make the IFA unreasonable unless it jeopardizes life or safety, which was not shown here.
rebuttals.quote: The RAD reasonably concluded that Ms. Ambroise failed to discharge that burden.

rebuttals.point: Procedural fairness was breached because the IFA was not raised at the outset of the hearing.
rebuttals.court_answer: Procedural fairness does not require the IFA to be raised at the outset, only that the claimant has an opportunity to respond.
rebuttals.quote: procedural fairness does not require that an IFA be raised at the outset of the hearing

authorities.authority: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
authorities.why: Sets out the reasonableness standard for administrative review.
authorities.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is justified, transparent and intelligible

authorities.authority: Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 1 FC 589 (CA)
authorities.why: Provides the two-prong IFA test and guidance on reasonableness.
authorities.quote: Both of these prongs must be satisfied to conclude that a refugee protection claimant does not have a viable IFA.

authorities.why: Sets out the presumption regarding state protection and well-founded fear.
authorities.quote: the Supreme Court does not require a panel to analyze state protection if the fear has not been established.

authorities.authority: Dezameau v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 559
authorities.why: Court found the RAD did not make the error described in Dezameau.
authorities.quote: the RAD did not make the error described in Dezameau, Josile or Desire.

authorities.authority: Alkhoury v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 153
authorities.why: Clarifies procedural fairness requirements regarding IFA notice.
authorities.quote: the issue of an IFA “is always an issue in a refugee hearing”

authorities.authority: Tariq v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 1017
authorities.why: Addresses timing of IFA notice and procedural fairness.
authorities.quote: the RPD “clearly raised” the IFA during the hearing

authorities.authority: Ranganathan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2001] 2 FC 164 (FCA)
authorities.why: Sets the high threshold for unreasonableness of an IFA.
authorities.quote: the applicant must establish “actual and concrete evidence” of conditions that “would jeopardize the life and safety”

authorities.authority: Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196
authorities.why: Clarifies that procedural fairness is not subject to reasonableness review.
authorities.quote: issues of procedural fairness should be analyzed outside the scope of judicial review

left_open.issue: Whether the correctness or reasonableness standard applies to RAD review of RPD procedural fairness breaches.
left_open.reason: Court resolves on basis of recent FCA authority but notes conflicting case law.
left_open.quote: Some decisions... have concluded that the correctness standard always applies... Other decisions have found that the reasonableness standard applies
